limits: Practitioner chapter with no experiments; company examples (COiN, GitLab Security Bot, Erica, ZoomInfo, Klarna) are anecdotes with no citations in the text.
Four-role ladder (executor, reviewer, collaborator, governor) and five agent scopes are the author's framing, not validated.
Autonomy levels are qualitative (Minimal, Moderate, High); no thresholds are given except illustrative ones.
Regulatory content (EU AI Act, GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOX) is brief and dates quickly.
practices: Progress humans through four roles, executor, reviewer, collaborator, governor, as agent autonomy grows (The Changing Role of Humans, Table 13-1).

Match interfaces to role: tight feedback loops for executors, dashboards, exception flags and confidence scores for reviewers, shared planning UI for collaborators, policy config, audit logs and explainability for governors (Table 13-1).
Involve stakeholders early as co-creators and define success metrics beyond technical performance (Aligning Stakeholders).
Tie each rollout expansion to concrete trust signals, as ZoomInfo did (Aligning Stakeholders).
Use progressive delegation: start with drafts or read-only access, expand autonomy as reliability is shown (Lifecycle of Trust).
Make trustworthiness visible with versioning, change logs, audit trails, surfaced uncertainty, and easy override (Lifecycle of Trust).
Provide trust repair: reset, retrain or restrict capabilities after mistakes (Lifecycle of Trust).
Scale governance with agent scope, from user-managed preferences for personal agents to multitier sign-off and governance board review for organizational agents (Table 13-3).
Apply RBAC so agents never exceed intended scope; personal agents may inherit user permissions, functional and organizational agents need explicit privileges (Agent Scope).
Scope memory: isolated by default for personal agents, shared access-controlled for team agents, policy-governed for org agents; let users inspect, delete and turn off memory (Shared Memory).
Define escalation thresholds by decision type, risk level or confidence, give the human context on escalation, and feed resolutions back into policies, retraining or prompts (Escalation Design).
Keep decision logs, user interaction logs and error logs, protect them with encryption and access control (Accountability Frameworks).
Run ongoing ethical audits and behavioral assessments, with independent third-party audits where possible (Accountability Frameworks).
Embed compliance in the pipeline: automated compliance gates, policy-as-code (e.g., Open Policy Agent), model cards and datasheets (Privacy and Regulatory Compliance).
Four closing principles: Experiment (pilot in a low-risk domain), Measure (define metrics first), Govern (oversight and logging early), Scale (iterate on trust and autonomy thresholds) (Conclusion).

terms.definition: Human uploads tasks and reviews every output; agent autonomy minimal when supervised.
Human spot-checks key outputs; agent autonomy moderate, handles routine work.
Human guides priorities and annotates jointly; agent autonomy high, drafts and executes with oversight.
Human sets policy, audits decisions, oversees escalation; agent has autonomy within governance rules.
Early in an agent's lifecycle, it should act cautiously, deferring to humans for review or approval. As it proves reliable, its autonomy can expand.
the policy and infrastructure layer that ensures agents don't act beyond their authority
Five scopes: personal, team, project, functional, organizational, with rising access, autonomy and risk.
structured evaluations designed to identify ethical risks, unintended consequences, and potential harm arising from agent behavior
